column1:
Examples of possible gender-
focused outcomes for  
energy sector
column2:
Examples of questions to consider 
to formulate project strategies and 
gender-related design features

• 	Are	women	currently	employed	
in the organization? If so, in 
what capacities? Are they well 
represented in the management, 
high-level committees, or  
the boards?
• 	Do	women	have	equal	access	to	
training opportunities? Is there a 
human resource strategy to promote 
gender equality?
• 	Has	any	gender	audit	been	
conducted? What are the findings 
and lessons learned from this?
• 	Does	the	organization	apply	good	
labor and safety standards? 
• 	Are	women’s	concerns	adequately	
reflected in the monitoring and 
supervision schemes?
column3:
• 	Train	officials	and	staff	(male	and	female)	
in gender issues of risk mitigation 
strategies, social safeguards, and all 
similar areas; in the development 
and implementation of action plans 
and programs; and in performance 
commitments. They should be able 
to apply the skills acquired from the 
training, and translate the skills to 
provision of improved gender- 
responsive services. 
• 	Ensure	implementation	of	any	gender-
related plans that may have come out  
of gender audits or gender action  
plans (GAPs).
• 	Establish	gender	sensitivity	and	secure	
work environment for women.
• 	Establish	mechanisms	to	institutionalize	
monitoring of existing gender equality 
principles in the workplace.

column1:
Enhanced women’s participation 
in decentralized, community-
based, and/or managed energy 
distribution models, and 
strengthened technical and 
organizational capacity
column2:
• 	Are	there	any	community-based	
energy distribution systems in 
the target area? If so, are women 
involved in them? Are women 
interested? What are the barriers to 
their participation?
• 	Are	there	women	with	the	required	
skill and education to manage this 
kind of community-based systems?
column3:
• 	Involve	women’s	NGOs	and	community-
based organizations in the activities.
• 	Train	women	to	be	employed	as	
operators, technicians, managers, etc.
• 	Provide	gender	training	to	existing	
institutions and the community to accept 
women as service providers.
• 	Conduct	gender-sensitive	user-education	
programs for consumers.
• 	Invest	in	research	and	development	on	
technical and socioeconomic aspects of 
rural energy systems.

column1:
Improved energy access for 
urban poor households in areas 
unserved by natural gas network 
(e.g., liquefied petroleum gas 
cylinders, municipal waste-based 
community biogas systems, 
improved cookstoves, etc.)
column2:
• 	What	is	the	nature	and	extent	of	
energy gap experienced by the target 
groups, and how are women affected 
by the lack of service?
• 	Is	building	of	gender	awareness	
required for project developers  
and designers?
• 	Is	gender-disaggregated	background	
information available?
• 	What	are	the	options	available	
for large-scale intervention? Are 
affordable proven technologies 
available? Are there existing 
marketing channels that can 
accommodate the new solutions? 
What other new channels can  
be developed?
column3:
• 	Engage	in	community	dialogues	to	
include views of both men and women 
about their needs and preferences, and 
various proposed technology options 
being offered. Identify the difference 
between women’s and men’s ability 
to participate during the problem 
identification and take necessary steps to 
solve them.
• 	Take	into	account	women’s	knowledge	
and their views about design features.
• 	Commission	baseline	studies	to	find	
out the situation on the ground and to 
collect and use sex-disaggregated and 
gender-specific data to raise awareness 
and inform program and project designers 
about women’s energy needs.
